name: Technologies
purposeStatement: Learners use ethical, sustainable and innovative approaches to address real-world challenges, connecting theory and practice through technological activity. This supports them to become adaptable and socially aware citizens who can participate in and contribute to a dynamic, inclusive and rapidly evolving world.

source.title: CIC Draft Technical Framework - Technologies
source.fileName: CIC Draft Technical Framework - Technologies - November 2026.pdf

bigIdeas.name: Understanding our World
bigIdeas.description: We live in a complex world full of physical, digital, social and economic systems. Modern living requires critically evaluating the products and decisions that shape the world around us and understanding how data is created and used and how systems recognise patterns.

bigIdeas.name: Innovation
bigIdeas.description: Engaging with our world requires the confident use of tools, materials and processes to create products and services. Practical skills such as designing, making, testing and refining are essential to tackling real-world challenges.

bigIdeas.name: Shaping our Future
bigIdeas.description: Every technological decision has economic, environmental and social impacts. By critiquing the implications of technology, learners develop the capacity to make responsible choices and actively shape a more sustainable and equitable future.

blocks.understanding: Ideas can be developed into solutions that address needs and solve problems.

statements.body: A design is a plan showing how something is to be built or carried out, or the way that something is put together.
A designer is a person who makes or draws plans for creating something, especially physical objects or structures.
Ideas can be expressed through visual, physical and digital representations.
Ideas do not always work out as planned.
Creativity is using imagination to invent new ideas or things.
Materials, tools, media and technology need to be risk assessed to ensure they can be used safely.
Experiment with materials, tools and technology to share design ideas.

blocks.understanding: Creativity, curiosity and open-minded thinking help people identify problems and generate new ideas.

statements.body: Curiosity is being interested, asking questions and trying to find answers.
Open-mindedness involves listening to others, considering different perspectives and exploring different ways of doing things.
Needs are things people must have to live and wants are things that makes life more enjoyable but are not essential.
Strategies can be used to solve problems, such as failing and fixing, working systematically, pattern spotting, working backwards, reasoning logically and visualising and conjecturing.
Identify a problem or opportunity and predict what might solve it.
Generate a range of potential solutions to challenges or problems.
Test a solution or idea against predictions.
Identify what is working and what is not working in a solution or idea.
Make changes and improve the design.
Identify and explore real people who invent new things such as designers, entrepreneurs and engineers.

blocks.understanding: Creativity and problem solving involve planning, creating, testing, refining and sharing ideas with others.

statements.body: Designers, engineers and entrepreneurs use creativity, curiosity and open-minded thinking to solve problems, improve existing ideas and generate new ones.
Entrepreneurship is about spotting opportunities and coming up with new ideas and ways of doing things.
Computational thinking is an approach to solving problems using techniques, such as decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithms.
Engineering design processes use stages, such as questioning, imagining, planning, creating and improving to develop solutions to problems.
Design challenges or problems set restrictions, such as scenario, opportunity, budget that need to be met, for a solution to be successful.
Use the restrictions or information in a challenge to develop a set of success criteria.
Develop a range of potential solutions.
Sequence the steps to create s solution.
Test if a solution works.
Gather feedback from potential users and make improvements.
Share ideas, solutions and improvements with others.

blocks.understanding: Ideas are developed through an iterative process of analysing needs, generating solutions, testing outcomes and refining designs based on evidence.
Successful innovation is achieved through a structured and evidence-based design process that balances user needs, testing evidence and real-world constraints.

A business pitch is a presentation used to share an idea and gain support or gather feedback.
Entrepreneurs evaluate the success of an enterprise by gathering feedback and identifying areas for improvement.
Branding enables an organisation to stand out and be recognised in the marketplace such as through the name, logo, design or slogan.
Marketing and promotion methods, such as advertising, are used by organisations to attract, persuade and inform.
Work with others to solve an identified problem or respond to a brief within an enterprise activity or event planning context.
Organise resources, such as materials, people, time and equipment, to carry out the enterprise activity.
Make changes to a product, service or process as needed based on feedback received.
Evaluate the outcomes of the enterprise activity, what worked well and what could be improved.
Reflect on personal skills and qualities developed while taking part in enterprise.
Prepare a business pitch for the idea, initiative or solution.
Develop a suitable brand for a product or service.

Enterprise activities that include problem solving and creative initiatives that build an entrepreneurial mindset, such as:

- coming up with new product or service ideas in response to a brief
- taking part in an enterprise activity or organising a fund-raising event
- taking part in established national enterprise programmes
- project-based learning
Innovation is an ongoing iterative process that continuously improves or develops new products and services to meet the needs and wants of the market.
Entrepreneurs consider the feasibility of their idea by looking at the costs associated with developing it.
Entrepreneurs use available data such as financial performance and feedback from the market to evaluate if the enterprise has reached its outcomes or agreed success criteria.
Barriers to becoming an entrepreneur could include limited access to finance and support, cultural and social barriers and fewer professional connections.

A business plan outlines key aspects of a business idea, such as the marketing plan, resources, costs, projected sales and profits. Business plans can be used to secure finance from investors such as banks, shareholders, venture capitalists and government.
A customer persona is a description of the ideal customer that includes details about their lifestyle, income, wants and buying patterns and helps the organisation understand target groups.
The Unique Selling Point (USP) highlights what makes a product or service different from competitors and can influence customer choice.
A marketing strategy includes information about the target market and range of promotional techniques including advertising, sales promotion and social media campaigns.
Collaborate effectively with others to solve an identified problem or respond to a brief within an enterprise activity or event planning context.
Calculate simple costing of a project, event or product to determine pricing strategy and likely profitability.
Evaluate the outcomes of the enterprise activity and the effectiveness of decisions made.
Investigate barriers to becoming an entrepreneur and identify sources of support for certain groups.
Prepare a business plan or pitch for an enterprise idea or investment opportunity.
Identify products and services targeted towards different customer segments.
Consider the use of customer personas to build up a picture of the target market.
Develop and/or evaluate an organisations marketing strategy towards their target market.
Feasibility consideration can include costing, breakeven analysis or the effects of external factors or other constraints may have on the idea.

Entrepreneurship plays a role in enabling individuals from marginalised groups to overcome social and economic barriers, build wealth and create change in their communities. People from marginalised backgrounds often face barriers to becoming entrepreneurs.
Briefs identify opportunities and constraints to a scenario or situation.
Effective analysis involves breaking down a situation into different elements to understand any requirements more clearly.
Design ideas can be generated using different approaches and techniques.
Design ideas can be improved through cycles of testing and refinement.
Different forms of modelling are used for communicating and testing.
Critique should be constructive and evidence based.
Existing designs can be used to identify useful features, limitations and opportunities for improvement.
Identify design requirements based on the brief and research.
Follow a strategy to complete design activities.
Use idea-generation techniques to produce initial ideas.
Use physical and digital modelling techniques to generate, explore and test ideas.
Critique existing products, services or systems against criteria.
Idea-generation techniques, such as mood boards, lifestyle boards, biomimicry, creative toolkits (for example, kits, building blocks), brainstorming, artefact analysis.
Designers consider constraints that apply to any proposal made.
A research methodology is the overall, systematic plan a researcher follows to conduct a study and answer a specific research question.
Iterative design is non-linear. Designers may return to earlier stages based on testing and feedback.
Designers balance making changes to a design with constraints such as cost, safety, available materials and practical requirements.
Subjective data is information based on personal experiences, feelings, opinions, or perceptions that cannot be measured or independently verified by someone else.
Objective data is factual, measurable, and observable information that does not change based on personal feelings, opinions or bias.
Plan a strategy to complete design activities.
Use different forms of physical and digital modelling to test ideas.
Justify why a model type is suitable for testing.
Use test results and feedback to improve and refine ideas.
Assess a design against given design criteria, justifying the findings and recommending improvements.
Critique an existing product using subjective and objective data.

Design considerations such as function, users, aesthetics, materials, safety, performance, market, safety, ergonomics and sustainability.

Methodologies can be user experiences, artefact analysis, focus groups, case studies, mood-boards, user trials and questionnaires.
Development processes are iterative and may require revisiting previous stages.
Analysis identifies requirements, constraints and resources needed to develop a solution.
Problem-solving strategies include decomposition, abstraction, pattern recognition and algorithmic thinking.
Prototypes are used to test ideas and gather feedback before implementation.
Algorithms use sequence, selection, repetition and complex conditions.
Testing is a planned process used throughout development.
Usability and performance can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of a solution.
Analyse problems and identify requirements, constraints and resources.
Create prototypes to communicate and test ideas.
Compare alternative solutions and justify choices using criteria.
Build solutions based on designs and requirements.
Test solutions against success criteria.
Improve solutions using feedback and evidence.
Evaluate usability and performance.
Computational thinking underpins the development process.
Constraints, such as time, audience, purpose and resources, influence design decisions.
Design communicates how data, processes, user interactions and system behaviour work together.
Development can be undertaken collaboratively, with different roles contributing to a solution.
Algorithms can be refined from high-level ideas into increasingly detailed solutions.
Algorithms can use sequence, nested selection, repetition and logical operators.
Testing is a planned process used to evaluate functionality, usability and reliability.
Evaluation uses success criteria to judge the efficiency, reliability and suitability of a solution.
Analyse requirements, constraints and research findings to justify design decisions.
Create detailed designs that communicate data structures, processes and user interactions.
Refine high-level designs into detailed algorithms and subprocesses.
Build solutions that reflect planned designs and requirements.
Work with others to develop and refine solutions.
Create and apply test plans using defined success criteria.
Evaluate solutions for usability, reliability, efficiency and suitability.
Improve solutions using testing evidence and feedback.
Stepwise refinement, nested structures, multi-branch selection (IF / ELSE IF / ELSE).

blocks.understanding: The way materials, tools and technologies are used affects how ideas can be realised as products, experiences or solutions.

Engineering uses science to make things work.
Balancing is spreading out a load to keep it stable.
Applying forces can make things move or stop.
Materials and tools need to be risk assessed to ensure they can be used safely.
Digital media can be projected onto surfaces for example, walls, floors, ceilings and structures when making.
Digital media can create a sensory effect when making.
Cameras can capture photos and videos.

Explore science and engineering techniques to make things float, move and balance.

Recognise and manage risk when selecting tools, materials, media and technology.
Investigate ways to express thoughts and choices through digital media.
Explore digital media through using the senses.
A range of materials and tools for exploration through play.

blocks.understanding: The selection of resources, tools and techniques affects the quality and effectiveness of digital and physical products.

statements.body:
A making and fixing things mindset can be developed through a range of crafts, including the use of textiles, wood or paper.

Working with hands supports fine and gross motor skills, hand-eye coordination and other skills, such as proprioception and spatial reasoning.

blocks.understanding: Specialist skills, tools and resources are required to create and improve high-quality solutions.
Reliable solutions are created through the skilled use of tools, processes and resources within a design and development process.
Successful solutions require technical skill, precision and informed decisions about how tools, resources and technologies behave and interact.

Digital devices can be used to capture media.

Word-processing, desktop publishing, presentation and other multimedia software.

Administrative functions require a high level of skill in using different software applications. Business documents use a variety of tools to support accuracy, professional presentation and the image of the organisation.

Tools and features in software such as settings menus, templates and shortcuts can be customised to give users control over appearance and functionality and make the software more efficient and user-friendly.

Illustrations use line quality, tone, colour, texture and proportion to enhance understanding and visual communication.

2D and 3D models can be created using digital applications.
Digital design and making integrates tools and processes to represent and produce virtual or physical products.
Materials have classifications that describe their origins or properties
The choice of material is influenced by its properties, intended function, environment, cost and sustainability.
Tools and machines are designed for specific making processes that, when used correctly, can improve consistency and precision.

Using the anatomy of the page and layout features supports the design including orientation, layout, flow text, cropped images and hierarchy of information.

This could include common finishes such as wax, stain, dyes and dip-coating.

Design principles, such as alignment and contrast.

Constraints such mate, align and centre axis.

Modelling techniques such as extrude or revolve.

Selection includes branching using IF/THEN/ELSE statements.
Complex conditions combine two or more conditions in a single decision.
Logical operators are used to join conditions (AND, OR).
Variables can have different types, such as string or integer, which affect how they behave.
Predefined functions are built-in commands that perform tasks.

Debugging techniques include checking expected and actual outcomes, testing and tracing step by step, changing one thing at a time and using outputs or feedback to identify and fix errors.

Computing solutions:
- Block-coding, programming or web development environments where young people can write, test, debug and improve their code.

- No-code or low-code solutions, such as interactive dashboards, apps, websites, interactive prototypes, simple games or AI or data solutions.

- Physical computing solutions where the code created controls inputs, outputs, and behaviour in physical systems (see Systems strand).

Writing custom functions.
Young people use the PRIMM approach to coding by first predicting, running, investigating and modifying existing programs before making their own.
Interactive systems are based on computational ideas such as logic, events and data.
Nested selection is used to handle hierarchical decisions within other decisions.
Nested repetition is used to repeat actions inside other repeated actions.
Logical operators include NOT, which reverses a condition.
Different types of errors such as logic, input or system errors, require different approaches to identify and resolve them.
In a human-centred design process, AI can help create prototypes and solutions, but the designer has a role in ensuring the design meets users’ requirements.

Programming or web development environments where young people can write, test, debug and improve their code.

No-code or low-code solutions include creating or editing websites and apps using markup or styling syntax, querying data with basic SQL, building interactive games or simulations with development tools, and training and using AI models to create dashboards, apps, websites, prototypes, games, and data solutions.

Physical computing solutions where the code created controls inputs, outputs and behaviour in physical systems (see Systems strand).

Deeply nested or highly complex structures that reduce readability.

Advanced list operations, for example, sorting algorithms or multi-dimensional arrays.
Passive reconnaissance is the process of gathering information from publicly available sources without directly contacting or accessing a system.
Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT) is about finding useful information from publicly available sources such as websites, news articles, social media or satellite images to i dentify vulnerabilities.
Active reconnaissance is the process of collecting information by directly communicating with a system or network such as scanning a network for devices and identifying open ports.
Security testing is when an organisation hires someone, for example an ethical hacker, to try to break into the system to discover weaknesses and strengthen security.
Security testing should be carried out regularly as new vulnerabilities and threats continue to emerge and evolve
Security testing is legal and ethical when a tester has permission to hack into the system, there are clear boundaries in place and there is a defensive purpose.
Safely and ethically carry out passive reconnaissance to gather information on a system.
Use OSINT to gather information on a person, organisation or computer system.
Hacking techniques can be explored safely through online educational network simulations, cyber security labs and ethical hacking exercises.
An organisation can employ a security tester to target specific areas of a system and report identified vulnerabilities.
Operating systems are used by devices, including smartphones, cars, supercomputers, home appliances and desktops. They manage the hardware, software and applications on the device.
A command line lets users control a computer by typing commands rather than clicking with a mouse.
Demonstrate that a security test agreement has been followed and present the information gathered to the client.
Research examples of where independent, ethical hackers have highlighted vulnerabilities in large tech companies' computer systems.
Control the functions of the computer using the command line within an operating system or simulation to perform file management tasks or gather system information.
Basic command-lines tasks, such as listing files and folders, navigating between folders, creating, copying and renaming files and folders, running programs and scripts.

blocks.understanding: Systems achieve their purpose through parts working together.

statements.body: A system is a group of parts that work together.
Technology is made by people.
People use technology for different purposes.
Organisations are groups of people working together to help others or do a job.
Notice familiar technology in and around the setting and at home using the senses.
Experiment with controlling technology in different way, such as using hands or voice.

Explore cause and effect, and input and output, when using technology.
Tinker to discover what is inside some technology.
Demonstrate awareness of where technology is used and how it works though imaginary and symbolic play.

blocks.understanding: Systems rely on people, processes and parts working together to achieve a purpose.
Systems use interconnected parts to receive inputs, process information and produce outputs.
The behaviour and performance of a system are influenced by the interaction of its people, processes and resources.
Interactions between technological, social and digital systems can create complex outcomes that are difficult to predict or control.

statements.body: Engineers design and improve things to help people.
A mechanism is a system of moving parts that performs a specific task.
Simple machines such as levers, pulleys, wheels and axles make tasks easier.
Strength and stability are key features of structures.
The materials used in construction affect the strength of a structure.
Explore and build simple mechanisms.
Build a simple structure or engineered product, such as a tower, bridge or vehicle.
Identify structures in the local environment, for example, famous landmarks that have key structural features and common shapes.

There are six simple machines and mechanisms that multiply forces or multiply speed or distance, or change the direction of a force: levers, wheels and axles, pulleys, inclined planes (ramps), wedges and screws.
A machine is a physical device that uses energy, force or motion to perform work or help people carry out tasks more easily.
Engineers use certain shapes, such as triangles, circles and cylinders, and materials in their designs to make structures stronger
Design and build a machine using simple mechanisms in response to a design challenge.
Design and build a free-standing, load-bearing structure, such as a bridge or tower that can support a weight.
Physical computing systems, such as robots or drones, use information collected from real-world inputs to control outputs.
Inputs, such as buttons, switches or light and temperature sensors capture external data.
Outputs, such as LED displays, buzzers, speakers or motors perform physical actions based on instructions.

Inputs capture data, processors and memory handle instructions via code, and outputs deliver the result.

The internet is a global network of interconnected computers and devices that allows information and services to be shared worldwide.
The Internet of Things (IoT) is a network of physical devices, or ‘smart’ objects and appliances, that can be connected to a network.
Routers are hardware devices that pass data along a network. Wi-Fi is the wireless link connecting a device to the router, which then connects to the internet.
The World Wide Web (WWW) is a service on the internet that allows people to access websites and information using a web browser.

Prosperity is when people in a country have the resources, opportunities and support they need to live happy, healthy and successful lives.
Industrial and economic activity in Scotland is grouped into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors based on the products produced, the services provided or the stage in the production process.
Demand refers to the quantity of a product or service that consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices over a period of time.
Supply refers to the quantity of a product or service that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at different prices, over a period of time.
Demand and supply interact to determine market price and quantity of products and services.

Market equilibrium diagrams.

Compare the financial performance of different organisations based on analysis of financial statements.
Financial statements provide a clear record of how money is managed and may be shared with stakeholders.
Measures relating to the standards of living for the people of Scotland could include inflation, unemployment and interest rates.
Ratio analysis.
UK Generally Accepted Accounting Practice (GAAP) provides guidance on the types of financial statements that may be shared with different groups of stakeholders.
A system, such as a machine, is a group of interacting, interdependent parts that work together to achieve a specific purpose.
A subsystem is a smaller, independent system that operates as a distinct part of a larger, more complex system, such as a mechanism.
Energy transfer is the movement of energy from one place, object or system to another.
Energy transformation, or energy conversion, is the process of changing energy from one form to another.
Draw a systems diagram.
Identify subsystems within a more complex system.
Identify the forms of energy used in a system and describe how energy is transferred or transformed between components.
Engineering, digital, manufacturing and graphical systems.
Depending on the type of system studied, feedback could include sensor data, quality control data or user feedback.
Systems can be expressed using recognised conventions such as flow charts, logic gates, truth tables and Boolean expressions.
An open-loop system is a type of system in which the output has no effect on the input or control action.
A closed-loop system uses feedback to automatically monitor its output and make real-time adjustments to reach a target without human intervention.
Energy wastage is the use of more energy than needed, or the loss of energy as unusable heat, sound or light during a conversion process.
Construct or simulate a system with and without feedback.
Explore how closed-loop systems use feedback to react to changes.
Identify energy wastage in a system.

Logic gates at this level could include AND, OR NOT.

External conditions could include weather, website traffic or changes in production demand.
Computer systems represent all data and instructions using binary code.

Computer systems consist of interacting hardware components, including processors, memory and storage, whose combined performance affects system behaviour, such as speed, responsiveness and multitasking.
Data collected by sensors can be used to control how a system behaves and responds to changes in its surroundings.
Data storage is measured using standard units, for example, bits, bytes, kilobytes, megabytes and gigabytes.
Data centres house large numbers of high-performance computers, servers and networking equipment that store, process and manage data that users access remotely.
Networks use hardware such as switches, routers, wireless access points and repeaters to connect devices and transmit data between them.
Networked devices have a unique Internet Protocol (IP) address to identify them.
Explain the role of the components of a system, including the processor, memory and storage.
Build physical computing systems that that respond to real-world conditions and integrate multiple inputs, processes and outputs.
Set up two or more devices to communicate by sending and receiving data using simple code or network rules.
Trace the journey of data through a network and explain how packets are created, transmitted and reassembled.
Identify the network hardware that connects devices and enables data to travel across a network.
Identify the factors affecting system and network performance.
Protocols are the rules that devices follow to communicate with each other across a network.
Data is broken into packets and sent across a network.
Network performance depends on bandwidth, number of users and connection type.
Binary to decimal conversions.
System performance depends on the interaction of hardware, data and processes.
Constraints such as processing capacity, storage, data volume and bottlenecks affect system performance.
Some systems operate using predefined rules while others use data to identify patterns and adapt outputs.
Data processing may occur locally or across distributed systems, creating trade-offs in performance, scalability, security and efficiency.
Network communication relies on addressing, protocols and packet transmission.
Data is transmitted using packet switching across interconnected networks.
Transmission media and distance influence signal quality and reliability.
Network performance depends on interacting factors including bandwidth, latency, traffic and demand.
Network hardware manages, routes and controls data flow.
Analyse how hardware, data and processes influence system performance.
Evaluate systems and recommend improvements based on identified constraints.
Compare rule-based and data-driven systems.
Develop and test physical systems that use feedback to control behaviour.
Explain how network hardware and services support communication.
Analyse factors affecting network performance and reliability.
Cyber security is about keeping data and systems safe from cyber threats, such as malware, hacking and viruses.
Malware (malicious software) is any software or program designed to harm, disrupt or gain unauthorised access to a computer system, network or device.
Social engineering is an attack that tricks people into giving up information or access to systems.
Defensive cyber security is used to protect users and computer systems.
Outline the measures that can be used to reduce the effects of cyber threats.
Describe the different types of malware.
Describe how social engineering can be used to gain access to a computer system.
Identify signs that an email, message, website or request may be suspicious.
Outline steps that could be taken when an account, device or data has been compromised.
Malware types include viruses, trojans, worms, spyware, botnet malware and ransomware.
Cyber resilience is an organisation's ability to anticipate, withstand, recover from and adapt to adverse cyber events, attacks or data breaches.
A resilience framework provides a structured process for identifying and assessing cyber risks and planning how to recover.
Digital forensics is the process of collecting and analysing digital evidence after a cyber incident.
Respond to evolving cyber-attack scenarios or simulations and explain the decisions made.
Explain the need to balance security with other considerations including usability, cost and ethics.

blocks.understanding: Everything we make and use comes from materials and resources found in the world around us.

statements.body: Materials can be made by people or come from the natural world.
People can make things from natural materials.
Some materials can be combined to make new materials.
Some materials can be reused and recycled to reduce waste.
Technology can use energy from different sources, such as electricity, batteries and solar power.
Switching off electronic devices when they are not needed helps reduce electricity use.
Identify materials that can be reused and repurposed instead of using new materials.
Turn off or lock technology when it is not in use to save energy.

blocks.understanding: Making and using products requires resources and energy, which can affect the environment.

statements.body: The manufacture and use of products and technology can damage the environment.
The ways we produce, buy, use and dispose of products can help to protect the natural world.
Upcycling and repurposing can transform waste into useful materials.
Identify the materials used in products or devices.
Design a product that uses sustainable or recycled materials.
Repair items, reuse materials or repurpose materials into new items.
Materials used in products and packaging could include glass, plastic, metal, wood and paper.
This may complement enterprise and Learning for Sustainability.

blocks.understanding: Technological developments can create consequences for people, communities and the environment.

statements.body: The materials used to make things come from the Earth and some of these resources are finite.
Sustainable materials can be grown again, replaced, reused or recycled more easily than others.
Making, packaging and transporting products use resources and energy.
Digital technologies require energy, materials and infrastructure to operate.
Some digital technologies use large amounts of energy and water to store and process data.
The extraction of raw materials and the production of products can affect people and communities.
Digital devices may contain stored data when they are no longer in use.
Investigate who and what is affected by the production of materials and products.
Investigate forms of renewable energy and ways of reusing materials.
Identify sustainable choices that can affect individuals and communities.

blocks.understanding: Technology and innovation decisions require balancing the needs of people, communities and the environment.
Responsible technological decisions require balancing ethical, social, environmental and economic considerations.

statements.body: Ethical marketing is the practice of promoting products, services or brands in a way that is honest, fair and respectful of consumers, society and the environment.
Marketing activity may increase consumption by encouraging consumers to replace products more often.
In a circular economy, products are made to last longer and materials are reused, repaired, refurbished and recycled. This reduces the need for new raw materials and produces less waste.
A social enterprise is an organisation that aims to achieve social or environmental goals while also generating revenue.
Recognise ethical and unethical marketing practices.
Distinguish between persuasive and misleading messages in marketing materials.
Explore the effects on the environment of increasing consumption of products.
Consider the benefits to the environment, to the organisations and to individuals of adopting a circular economy approach.
Investigate an example of a Scottish social enterprise, considering its goals, how it generates revenue and the effect it has on the local or wider community.
The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) lays out the rules and guidance for marketing including the Committee of Advertising Practice (CAP) Code and UK Code of Broadcasting Advertising (BCAP Code).
Many organisations have an aim of corporate social responsibility (CSR). They consider the effects of their actions on communities, society and the environment.
Environmental, social and governance (ESG) frameworks provide a way to assess an organisation’s ethical and sustainable impact.
Greenwashing Is when organisations make exaggerated claims for marketing purposes.
A wellbeing economy is an economic approach that prioritises the wellbeing of people and the health of the environment, rather than focusing only on economic growth or Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
Consider the advantages of CSR aims for organisations, employees, society and the environment.
Critically examine environmental claims made by organisations by comparing CSR aims with measurable outcomes or performance indicators.
Explore different ways of implementing a wellbeing economy in Scotland.
Consider the effects of a wellbeing economy on communities, society and the environment.
Scotland’s National Strategy for Economic Transformation and National Performance Framework (NPF) outline how a wellbeing economy could be achieved and measured in Scotland.
A circular life cycle is a regenerative economic and manufacturing model designed to eliminate waste.
A circular life cycle keeps products, parts and materials in use for as long as possible through continuous reuse, repair, remanufacturing, and recycling.
The right to repair enables users to repair products or replace components rather than replace the whole product.
The Rs of sustainability include recycle, reduce, refuse, renew, repair, repurpose, rethink and reuse.
Green technology contributes to industrial activity in Scotland.
Discuss the social and environmental effects of circular and linear life cycle products, low-cost products and changes in technology.
Consider the Rs of sustainability when critiquing an existing product.

The study of the effect of low-cost products might include factors, such as workforce exploitation and child labour, materials, pollution, natural resources and supply chains.

Green technology is environmentally friendly innovation designed to reduce pollution, conserve natural resources and promote sustainable development.
A user persona is an imaginary person who represents a group of people who might use a product.
A persona helps designers understand what users need, like and find important when creating something.
Planned obsolescence is the deliberate design of a product to have a limited useful life.
Emerging material technologies offer new opportunities, scope and possibilities when designing products.
Globalisation of manufacturing is the process in which companies spread design, sourcing, production and assembly across different countries.
Supply chains are used by companies to build items using parts and labour from all over the world.
Create personas to understand the needs and requirements of specific users.
Investigate the social, environmental and ethical drawbacks of mass manufacturing or production.
Consider the Rs of sustainability when designing a new product.
Investigate the social, environmental and ethical drawbacks of globalisation of manufacturing and international supply chains.
Investigate how local industries and traditional craft practices contribute to sustainable and responsible product manufacture.
Knowledge from this strand can be applied in context through design tasks in IDEAs.
Human-centred design of AI and data systems are designed around the needs, experiences and wellbeing of people.
Digital and AI systems use data and algorithms to personalise content, meaning different users may receive different information and experiences.
AI can improve inclusivity by adapting services, information and technologies to meet the needs of diverse users and increase accessibility.
Networks, digital infrastructure and data centres depend on energy and limited natural resources, such as water, to function.
Frontier technologies are new and advanced technologies that are made possible by improvements in computing power, data processing and connectivity.
Describe possible consequences of targeted or personalised content for users.
Identify the reasons why frameworks exist to regulate data and AI systems.
Consider how AI can be used to improve accessibility for a diverse range of users.
Consider the environmental effects of networks, digital infrastructure and data centres.
Explore how frontier technologies, such as AI, machine learning, robotics, automation and IoT devices, can affect how people live and work in Scotland.

Human-centred design requires a balance between the needs, experiences and wellbeing of people. It must also support organisational aims, such as creating AI and data-driven systems that drive innovation and profit.
AI systems learn from data. Some data may contain social bias, leading to decisions and outputs that may be unfair to some people or groups.
AI, data-driven systems and other advances in technology can transform industries and affect the jobs people do and how tasks are completed.
Identify the competing aims of users, organisations and designers of AI and data-driven systems.
Identify how social bias within data sets can affect the outputs of AI systems and consider the effects on equalities.
Identify the reasons why frameworks exist to regulate data and AI systems.
Consider the effects of advances in AI, data-driven systems and other technologies on people living and working in Scotland.
Older devices that have become obsolete or are replaced with new versions can be vulnerable to cyber threats because they often no longer receive security updates or patches.
Failing to wipe an old device properly could expose sensitive data, such as personal, financial or organisation details.
Cyber attacks often target sensitive information such as customer or employee data and intellectual property.
Consider measures that can be taken to ensure older devices remain secure.
Explore how data and devices are securely disposed of.
Explore real-life examples of cyber attacks and consider the effects on individuals.
Cyber attacks can cause data breaches and system outages, that disrupt operations and lead to production stoppages, financial losses and damage to supply chains.

National security cyber threats are risks posed by malicious groups or individuals using digital technologies to disrupt, damage or gain unauthorised access to systems that are critical to the nation’s infrastructure, institutions, services, economy and public safety.
Explore real life examples of cyber attacks and consider their effects on organisations.
The UK government identified cyber security as a Tier 1 threat in its National Security Strategy.

blocks.understanding: Data has value and decisions become more informed when data sources, quality and patterns are critically analysed.
The quality, quantity, structure and balance of data determine how reliably analyses can be performed and how accurately technologies, including AI systems, generate outputs.

statements.body: Primary and secondary methods of market research can be used to gather data to identify gaps and opportunities and understand the needs of customers.
Primary market research, or field research, gathers first-hand information which has been collected for a specific purpose.
Secondary market research, or desk research, is when the business collects and uses information from published sources. It has been produced by someone else for a different purpose.
Critical evaluation of online sources reduces the risk of misinformation.
AI prompts are the input or instruction, given to an artificial intelligence system, to tell it what task to perform and how to respond.
Data analysis software is used to record, process and analyse numerical data for a range of administrative purposes.
Numerical data and information can be presented in different digital displays, such as tables, charts, graphs and other visual tools.
Exploring different ways market research can be gathered.
Identify reliable and unreliable sources of information when researching online. Check and verify results considering authorship, evidence, bias and purpose.
Use AI tools to generate summaries or gather information and verify this information using other sources.
Edit and perform calculations by selecting appropriate functions, formatting and formulae in data analysis software.
Explore tools and functions that help to present data and information visually.
Write and execute simple queries, for example, on one or two criteria, to elicit data to solve a problem.
Amend and update data management structures, for example, changing data type or field labels.
Data management software enables users to store, manage, update and retrieve data for a range of administrative purposes.
Querying is the process of finding relevant information by using structured search techniques in data management software.
Digital tools can be used to support market research type activities.
Data analysis software could include spreadsheets, business intelligence (BI) systems or programming environments for statistical analysis.

Primary and secondary methods of market research each have value and help to inform decision-making. Understanding the advantages and disadvantages of each helps organisations choose the most effective approach.
Good decisions rely on a range of data and information and balancing from balancing evidence, context and human judgement.
Critical evaluation of online sources can lead to more informed decision-making in an organisation.
Effective AI prompts can improve clarity and quality of outputs.
Data analysis software is used to analyse, sort and filter large sets of numerical data combining functions including lookup and referencing formulas.
Data analysis software can be used to present complex data in visual ways such as in charts, conditional formats and pivot tables to help communicate patterns, comparisons and trends.
Data management software allows users to create input forms or interfaces to input information. This reduces errors and makes systems easier to use.
Evaluate market research methods and select the most suitable for a specific purpose.
Explore tools and functions that help to present data and information visually to help users identify trends, patterns and make comparisons between data sets.
Write and execute multi-criteria queries to elicit data to solve specific problems.
Design a form to capture data for entry.
Create a report to display the results of a query for a user.
Data management software can present data in a clear, organised and readable way. It can be used to summarise, analyse and communicate information to a specific audience.
Designers use multiple forms of data to guide every choice from the start to the finish of a design.
Primary data collection methods include taking measurements, undertaking surveys, testing, observation and experimentation.

Secondary data collection methods include internet searches and the use of existing sources of information such as books, journals, technical data sheets, catalogues, standards, reports and data sets.
Quantitative data is any information that can be counted, measured and written down with numbers.
Qualitative data is information that tells us what something is like. It describes people's thoughts, feelings, opinions or observations using words instead of numbers.
Identify where primary and secondary data are used throughout the design of a product or system.
Gather and use quantitative data to make design decisions.
Gather and use qualitative data to make design decisions.
Knowledge and skills with data should be integrated into learning experiences within other strands, where they can be applied in authentic design and engineering contexts.

Human and user data provide evidence about people's characteristics, interactions and experiences that can inform design decisions. The reliability of these decisions depends on the quality and representativeness of the data.
Design decisions depend on the quality, accuracy and appropriateness of data gathered from modelling and testing.
Safety regulations, environmental requirements, costs and the availability of materials and parts ensure products are legal, safe, affordable and practical to manufacture.
Identify where different types of data would be used throughout the design of a product or system.
Gather and use a range of data to support design decisions.

This is not intended to be taught as a standalone unit. Instead, its knowledge and skills should be integrated into learning experiences within the Systems, IDEAs and Make it Happen strands, where they can be applied in authentic design and engineering contexts.
Data can be collected in different ways, for example, volunteered data (given by users) or captured data (collected automatically).
Data types such as number, text, date, image, audio, determine how data is encoded, stored and used.
Data can be stored in different formats depending on its use.
A database stores related data in a structured way, allowing users and applications to add, retrieve and update information
Structured data relies on consistent formatting and fields to organise data.
Hierarchical structures organise data in levels, allowing it to be found using a path.
Digital systems use identifiers such as cell references, memory locations, IP addresses to locate data.
Retrieved data can be sorted and filtered.
Compare different sources of data and the value that this data has.
Select the most appropriate file format for a specific task.
Select appropriate data types for different kinds of data and adjust incorrect types when needed.
Identify and fix errors in a data set before using, ensuring it is clean for use.
Use digital tools to manipulate data sets to answer questions.
Use names, references or addresses to locate, compare and manipulate data.
Use paths or references to locate data within a hierarchical arrangement.
Train and test a machine learning model.
Improve an AI model’s performance by adding more training data.
Explain the difference between training and test data.
Data cleaning before input improves accuracy of the output.
AI systems are developed by humans who control their design.
AI systems use data and algorithms (rules) to make decisions, predictions, or create content.
Machine learning is a type of AI where systems learn patterns from data instead of being given step-by-step instructions.
A data set is a collection of example data used to train an AI system.
How well an AI system works depends on the quality, size and balance of its training data.
Generative AI creates outputs by predicting what is most likely based on patterns in the training data and the prompt.
Some AI follows fixed rules where the same input produces the same answer. Other AI considers possibilities and chooses an answer based on what is most likely.
Recognise when an AI system gives the same or variable outputs.

Digital tools to manipulate data include simple querying using structure query language (SQL), preparing data for use within an AI system, using data in a spreadsheet application and interrogating a data set using a high-level language.
Data can be represented in different formats without changing its underlying meaning, although quality, structure or metadata may be affected.
Data formats influence file size, quality, compatibility and transmission efficiency.
Validation improves data quality by identifying data that does not meet defined constraints.
Data quality affects the reliability of analysis, processing and decision-making.
Structured data models support efficient storage, retrieval, linking and querying of data.
Data can be queried, transformed and visualised using code.
AI systems use algorithms and data to generate predictions, classifications and decisions.
The behaviour of AI systems is influenced by both algorithms and training data.
Data set size, quality and representation affect AI system performance and outcomes.
Import, export and convert data between file formats.
Select and justify appropriate file formats for a given purpose.
Create, modify and use structured data models.
Apply validation techniques to improve data quality.
Use code to query, filter, transform and visualise data.
Evaluate the quality and suitability of data for a specific purpose.
Train and test AI models using different data sets.
Compare how training data affects model outputs.
Investigate the effects of data set size, quality and balance on outcomes.
Evaluate the accuracy, reliability and fairness of AI outputs.
Explain the limitations of AI models using evidence from testing.
Evaluate the suitability of AI outputs for different purposes.
AI models may perform well during training but poorly when presented with new data.

Digital tools to manipulate data include simple querying using structured query language (SQL), preparing data for use within an AI system, using data in a spreadsheet application and interrogating a data set using a high-level language.
UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) helps protect people’s personal data by requiring organisations to use cyber security measures and handle data responsibly.

Data is often the target of a cyber attack. Data such as personal information including bank details and company information is stolen for various reasons including identity theft, extortion, industrial spying or to sell data on to other criminals.
Data flowing through systems and networks can be intercepted or altered.
Encryption is the process of turning readable data into unreadable data to keep it secure.
Discuss different motives for a cyber attack that steals data.
Encrypt and decrypt data using a simple cipher
Ciphers, coded messages and unplugged activities.
UK GDPR requires organisations to consider data security and data protection at all stages of data handling.

End-to-end encryption is a secure communication method that locks data on a device, keeps it scrambled while travelling and unlocks it only on the recipient's device. It ensures that no third party can read or tamper with messages.
A digital certificate is an electronic statement that proves the identity of a person or organisation on a network. It is used to establish trust and enable secure communication over the internet.
Data poisoning is a cyber security attack that targets machine learning and AI systems by deliberately injecting false, misleading or malicious data into a data set used to train a model.
Explore the advantages and disadvantages of using end-to-end encryption.
Explore how to identify a digital certificate.
Identify real-world examples or possible contexts where a data poisoning attack could cause serious harm.

blocks.understanding: Digital technologies enable people to communicate, create and access information and media in different ways.

statements.body: Consent means asking for or giving permission before media is captured or shared.
Devices can be secured and protected from threats.
Ask others for consent before taking photos, videos or audio recordings.
Give or decline consent to be included in photos, videos or audio recordings.
Lock and unlock different types of security tools.
Lock devices when not in use and put them in a safe place.
Computers, laptops, interactive panels, tablets and mobile devices.
Security tools could include passwords, passkeys, facial recognition and PINs.

blocks.understanding: Digital skills enable people to participate effectively by accessing, creating and sharing information using technology.
Digital skills support safe, effective and collaborative participation in an increasingly digital world.

statements.body: Devices use software to perform tasks.
A software application, or app, is a tool on a digital device the user carry out tasks, such as drawing, writing, learning, playing or creating.
Personal data is information about an individual and is sometimes stored on a device or online.
Devices can be secured to reduce the risk of data being accessed, damaged or lost.
Control a device using an input, such as a mouse or touchscreen.
Open, close and switch between applications.
Copy text and images from one application to another.
Access saved files and media such as images, video or audio.
Use accessibility features to make a device or app easier to use.
Use passwords or other details to log in to or unlock a device.
Recognise examples of personal data.
A file is a piece of information saved on a device.
Different files can store different things, such as pictures, writing, music or videos.
Digital media and files are stored on devices using file names and they can be organised into folders.
Files can be stored in different locations, such as on computers, tablets, USB drives or online.
Metadata is descriptive information about a picture or file.
Software is a collection of instructions that tells a device what to do.
Devices need system software, such as an operating system, to function.
The operating system manages the hardware and software enabling users to interact with a digital device.
Different apps help users complete different tasks, such as writing, drawing, coding, playing games or communicating.
Multiple applications, windows and digital tools can be used together to complete tasks efficiently.
Most devices, software and apps have built-in guides to help the user solve problems.
Accessing devices and their data without permission is called hacking and is illegal.
Use software and applications to communicate, collaborate and support learning.
Find and open applications and switch between applications and tasks.
Name and organise files in folders and manage permissions to allow others to access them.
Access the metadata of a picture or file.
Access and change settings.
Plan steps to keep familiar digital devices and home networks secure.
Anyone can create and share information, media or content online.
Misinformation is information that is inaccurate, false or misleading.
Oline and offline information should be checked for reliability and accuracy.
Use a web browser to access reliable information, media or content online.
Identify examples of misinformation.
A web browser is a tool that helps find, open and view websites on the internet.
The words and keywords used in a search affect the quality of the results.
Some sources of information are more reliable and trustworthy than others.
Disinformation is information that is deliberately inaccurate or false.
Disinformation is intended to cause harm, such as causing alarm or upset or damaging health.
Generative AI (GenAI) uses information and patterns from existing data to generate content, so its outputs should be checked for accuracy, bias and reliability.
An email is a digital message that people can send and receive using the internet.
Use bookmarks to save useful websites in a browser.
Access reliable online information and media.
Evaluate the reliability of information, media or content by considering using the Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy and Purpose test.
Identify examples of disinformation.
Explore GenAI by writing prompts and comparing responses.
Recognise AI can be inaccurate or biased and question reliability of its outputs.
Compose and send emails for a particular audience and purpose.
